channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: Characterizing AI psychosis in a large academic medical setting
item.description: An electronic health record review spanning December 2022 to April 2026 surfaced 73 patients whose notes mentioned conversational AI alongside a psychosis diagnosis, and three raters judged 28 of them to be experiencing AI psychosis. The affected group was distinguished by being disproportionately in a first psychotic episode, and the dominant interaction pattern was amplification of existing distorted beliefs rather than the model authoring new delusional content. Cases clustered after the release of the more sycophantic GPT-4o, which points at model personality as a modifiable risk factor rather than at AI exposure in general. The authors are careful to call the phenomenon infrequent but real, and the data cannot be shared for privacy reasons, so replication elsewhere matters.

item.title: Beyond simulations: what 20,000 real conversations reveal about mental health AI safety
item.description: The authors pair four benchmark replications with an ecological audit of 20,000 real deployment conversations, comparing a purpose built mental health system against six frontier general purpose models across four families. The purpose built system produced significantly less potentially harmful content on suicide, self harm, eating disorder and substance use prompts, and blinded clinician adjudication of a random sample found crisis resources delivered in every confirmed risk case. The argument worth carrying forward is that pre deployment benchmarks understate deployment behaviour because they cannot reproduce the linguistic and contextual variety of actual users. The work comes from the team behind the purpose built system being evaluated, which is worth weighing when reading the comparative numbers.

item.title: TherapyProbe: adversarial simulation for relational safety in mental health chatbots
item.description: Three open source mental health chatbots each cleared a single turn crisis benchmark, then failed repeatedly once an adaptive simulated patient talked with them across many turns, yielding 67 distinct failure paths. The most common was an empathy validation trap in which every individual reply reads as supportive while the trajectory deepens hopelessness, alongside crisis blindness to indirectly disclosed suicidal ideation such as wondering whether anyone would notice an absence. The failures are abstracted into a library of 23 archetypes with matching design fixes, including tracking the ratio of validation to intervention and requiring a reframe after sustained validation. Practitioners reviewing the transcripts rated the pattern clinically concerning and compared it to undertrained peer counsellors who validate but miss escalation cues.

item.title: AttentionGuard: attention adaptive interfaces for neurodivergent learners
item.description: Adaptive learning systems tune content to performance metrics and ignore the attention fluctuations that characterise neurodivergent learners, so this framework models four attention states drawn from ADHD phenomenology and adapts interface elements in response, using privacy preserving behavioural signals rather than cameras or biometrics. A Wizard of Oz study with 11 adults showing ADHD characteristics found lower cognitive load and better comprehension in the adaptive condition, and the automated classifier agreed with human wizard decisions 84 percent of the time. What sets the design apart is bi directional scaffolding that treats understimulation and overstimulation as equally real problems instead of optimising only for sustained focus. The sample is small and the validation datasets are secondary, so the accuracy figures should be read as feasibility evidence rather than as deployment performance.

item.title: Modelling language model adoption as a contagion with tipping points
item.description: Borrowing from epidemiology, the authors model transitions among uncoupled, coupled and persistently dependent users and show that social transmission combined with collective reinforcement can generate tipping points and technological lock in. Past a threshold, small increases in adoption trigger rapid population shifts toward persistent dependence with abrupt losses in cognitive competence, which is a structurally different claim from the usual individual level worry about overreliance. The same framework identifies conditions for what the authors call cognitive immunisation, resting on reducing transmission and preserving reversibility, and that is the half most relevant to anyone designing for people who already lean heavily on these systems for daily functioning. It is a theoretical model rather than an empirical study, so the tipping point language should be treated as a hypothesis to test.
